sections.b: Matthew gives Peter more space than any other Gospel. Only Matthew tells how Peter walked on the water toward Jesus, began to sink and cried "Lord, save me!" (Matthew 14:28–31). Peter asks Jesus to explain the saying about uncleanness (Matthew 15:15). At Caesarea Philippi he confesses Jesus as "the Messiah, the Son of the living God," and only Matthew records Jesus' answer: the new name Peter, the rock on which the church will be built, and the keys of the kingdom (Matthew 16:16–19). Moments later Peter rebukes Jesus for speaking of his death and is called "Satan" (Matthew 16:22–23). He witnesses the transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8), pays the Temple tax with a coin from a fish (Matthew 17:24–27), and asks how often he must forgive (Matthew 18:21). Matthew's Peter is the first disciple in faith and in failure alike.

common: Peter was the leader and spokesman of the Twelve.
Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is the turning point of the Synoptic Gospels.
uncommon: Some scholars think 16:17–19 was originally a resurrection appearance to Peter moved into Jesus' lifetime.

claude.title: The rock that sank
claude.body: Matthew's rare verb for Peter's sinking (14:30) returns only at 18:6 and is the verb the Greek of Exodus 15:4 uses for Pharaoh's officers sunk in the Red Sea, who went down "like a stone" (Exodus 15:5). I suspect Matthew wanted readers to remember the sinking when Jesus names Peter the rock: his foundation is the hand that caught him. This is a guess about word choice.

sections.b: Matthew sets the transfiguration six days after Peter's confession and Jesus' first prediction of his death (Matthew 17:1). He adds details that strengthen the link with Moses: Jesus' face "blazed like the sun" (compare Exodus 34:29–35), the cloud is "full of light," and the disciples fall face down until Jesus touches them and says, "Get up. Stop being afraid" (Matthew 17:6–7). The voice repeats the words of the baptism and adds Moses' words, "Listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15). Only Matthew calls the event "the vision" (Matthew 17:9). On the way down, Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 17:10–13).

common: The transfiguration previews Jesus' resurrection glory.
uncommon: Some scholars think the story began as a resurrection appearance.

sections.b: Matthew is the only Gospel to use the word "church" (Matthew 16:18; Matthew 18:17). In 16:19 Jesus gives Peter the keys of the kingdom and the power to bind and loose; in 18:18 the same power goes to the disciples together. Between them stands a three-step procedure for a brother who sins: correction in private, then before one or two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), then before the church (Matthew 18:15–17). If he refuses the church, he is to be treated "as the Gentile and the tax collector." The setting matters: the procedure follows the parable of the straying sheep and precedes the command to forgive seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:12–14; Matthew 18:21–35). The Dead Sea community had a strikingly similar rule of rebuke before witnesses (Leviticus 19:17).

common: The aim of discipline is to win the sinner back.
uncommon: Some read "treat him as a Gentile and tax collector" as a call to reach out to him as Jesus did to such people.

sections.b: Peter offers to forgive a brother seven times; Jesus answers "seventy-seven times," the number of Lamech's vengeance in Genesis 4:24, reversed into unlimited mercy (Matthew 18:21–22). The parable that follows contrasts a debt of ten thousand talents, forgiven by the king, with a debt of a hundred denarii that the forgiven slave refuses to forgive (Matthew 18:23–35). The ending repeats the warning that follows the Lord's Prayer: the Father will not forgive those who do not forgive others "from the heart" (Matthew 6:14–15; Matthew 18:35).

common: God's forgiveness comes first, and forgiving others is the response.
uncommon: Some read 18:34 as support for purgatory.

sections.h: Herod Antipas and the death of John
sections.b: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC to AD 39. Matthew tells how he had John the Baptist arrested for condemning his marriage to Herodias, the wife of his half-brother (Leviticus 18:16), and beheaded at his birthday feast after a rash oath to Herodias's daughter (Matthew 14:1–12). Josephus agrees that Antipas killed John, though he gives a political motive: fear that John's following would lead to revolt. Matthew calls Antipas "king" in 14:9 by popular usage, and shows him fearing that Jesus is John raised from the dead.

sections.h: John's death and John as Elijah
sections.b: Matthew 14:1–12 tells of John's imprisonment and beheading by Herod Antipas, and his disciples' burial of his body. His death foreshadows Jesus': both are prophets, both are held by rulers who fear the crowd, and both are executed by rulers who seem reluctant (Matthew 14:5, 9; Matthew 27:24). After the transfiguration Jesus says that Elijah has already come and been mistreated, and the disciples understand that he means John (Matthew 17:10–13; compare Matthew 11:14; Malachi 4:5).

In the dispute about hand-washing, Jesus says that what enters the mouth does not make a person unclean, but what comes out of the heart (Matthew 15:11, 17–20). Mark's version adds "With this he made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19); Matthew leaves that out and ends with hand-washing (Matthew 15:20). Many scholars therefore think Matthew's church still kept the food laws, while most Christians read the saying as setting them aside, as Acts 10 and Romans 14:14 do.

Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem ask why Jesus' disciples break "the tradition of the elders" by eating with unwashed hands. Jesus answers that they break God's command for their tradition: a vow of korban could free a man from supporting his parents, against the commandment to honor them (Matthew 15:1–6; Exodus 20:12). He quotes Isaiah 29:13 on worship that is only human rules. Christians have appealed to this passage in debates over the place of church tradition (see the card at Matthew 15).

In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman, from Israel's ancient enemies, begs Jesus to heal her daughter. He says he was sent only to "the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost" and that the children's bread is not for the little dogs. She answers that the dogs eat the crumbs, and Jesus praises her "great faith" (Matthew 15:21–28). Like the centurion (Matthew 8:5–13), she shows Gentile faith before the mission to all nations (Matthew 28:19).

Jesus warns against looking down on the "little ones," because "their angels in heaven are always looking on the face of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 18:10). The image is of courtiers with access to the king (Esther 1:14). This verse, with Psalm 91:11 and Acts 12:15, is the main biblical basis for belief in guardian angels. At Matthew 16:27 the Son of Man comes "with his angels" to judge.

In Matthew the parable of the hundred sheep is told to the disciples about "little ones" in the community who stray (Matthew 18:12–14); in Luke it answers critics of Jesus' welcome of sinners (Luke 15:3–7). Both draw on Ezekiel 34, where God promises to search for the strays that Israel's shepherds neglected. Jesus also says he was sent to "the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost" (Matthew 15:24).

Jesus promises that "the gates of Hades will not be stronger than" his church (Matthew 16:18). Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the world of the dead, and "the gates of death" or "of Sheol" is an Old Testament image (Job 38:17; Psalm 9:13; Psalm 107:18; Isaiah 38:10). Most readers take the promise to mean that death will not defeat the church; some read it of the church breaking into death's realm to free its prisoners.

In the warning about snares, Jesus says it is better to enter life maimed than to be thrown into "the eternal fire" or "the fire of Gehenna" (Matthew 18:8–9). The saying repeats Matthew 5:29–30 in the setting of community life, where some read hand, foot and eye as members of the church who lead others astray.

The yearly half-shekel paid by Jewish men for the Temple was based on Exodus 30:11–16. In Matthew 17:24–27 collectors ask whether Jesus pays it. Jesus answers that kings' sons are free, yet pays for himself and Peter with a stater from a fish's mouth, "so that we do not trip them up." After the Temple's destruction in AD 70, Rome took the same tax from Jews for the temple of Jupiter.

Matthew tells two feedings in a wilderness place: five thousand men with five loaves (Matthew 14:13–21) and four thousand with seven (Matthew 15:32–39). Both recall God feeding Israel with manna (Exodus 16) and Elisha feeding a hundred men with twenty loaves (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus later asks the disciples to remember the bread (Matthew 16:9–10), as Moses asked Israel to remember the manna (Deuteronomy 8:2–3).

sections.b: Jesus comes to his disciples "walking on the sea" (Matthew 14:25), doing what the Old Testament says God alone does: God "tramples on the back of the Sea" (Job 9:8) and makes a road through the waters (Psalm 77:19). His words "I am" echo God's self-naming, and the disciples respond by worshiping him as God's Son (Matthew 14:33).

sections.h: Elijah on the mountain and in John
sections.b: Elijah appears with Moses at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3). The disciples then ask why the scribes say Elijah must come first (Malachi 4:5–6), and Jesus answers that Elijah has come already and been mistreated, meaning John the Baptist (Matthew 17:10–13). Some people thought Jesus himself was Elijah (Matthew 16:14).

The transfiguration recalls Moses on Sinai: six days, a mountain, three companions, a cloud, a voice, a shining face (Exodus 24; Exodus 34:29–35). Moses himself appears with Elijah (Matthew 17:3), and the voice's "Listen to him" applies to Jesus Moses' promise of a prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15).

At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16). Jesus orders silence (Matthew 16:20) and immediately begins to teach that he must suffer, die and rise (Matthew 16:21). Peter's protest shows how far a suffering Messiah was from common expectation.
